turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, um, what finally scared me into coming in is that I just keep making these really dumb technical mistakes at work. I know better than to make them, too. 

I’m a camera operator and editor, and we just had this massive project for a corporate client—actually, they were honestly the worst. The main producer kept changing his mind about the lighting setup, and then he brought his dog to set, which was this adorable little French bulldog, but it kept trying to chew on the XLR cables. I love dogs, I actually grew up with a golden retriever named Buster, but you just can't have them running around C-stands and heavy equipment, you know? It’s a huge safety liability. Plus the catering was just awful, it was just these sad, soggy wraps... 

But anyway... wait, why was I talking about the dog? Oh, right, my mistakes. Yeah. So I've been doing things like labeling the camera cards wrong, or just completely missing a timecode note from the director. The worst one recently was I exported a final client cut and it had the completely wrong lower-third graphic on it. And the crazy part is, I *checked* it before exporting. I stared right at it. I just... I don't know how I keep missing this stuff, but it's really starting to freak me out.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless technical mistakes at work, such as mislabeling cards, missing notes, and exporting cuts with wrong graphics despite checking them.

turns.doctor_question: When you're making these mistakes at work, does it feel more like you're having trouble focusing or paying attention to the details, or does it feel more like you're worried or anxious about making mistakes?
turns.patient_response:
I think... it's definitely the focus thing. I'm not really an anxious person, usually. It's just like I can't hold onto the details. Like I was saying with that lower-third graphic? I literally stared right at it on my monitor before I exported it. The font was completely wrong—it was Arial instead of Helvetica. 

Which, honestly, why do corporate clients obsess over Helvetica so much? There’s literally an entire documentary just about that one font. My friend Sarah made me watch it back in film school. She was a total typography nerd, she even got this huge ampersand tattooed on her wrist. I always thought about getting a tattoo, maybe like a little vintage camera lens or a clapperboard, but I can never commit to a design because what if I hate it in ten years? 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the mistakes. Yeah, no, it's not worry. I just... I look right at the wrong label on a camera card or a missed timecode note, and my brain just completely glazes over the details even when I'm trying to pay attention.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient confirms they have trouble focusing on details, stating their brain 'glazes over the details' leading to careless mistakes like missing wrong fonts or labels.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a tangent about fonts, documentaries, and tattoos before forgetting the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies that their mistakes are driven by anxiety, stating 'I'm not really an anxious person' and 'it's not worry'.

turns.doctor_question: Have you always had trouble with focus and attention to details like this, or is this something that's gotten noticeably worse recently?
turns.patient_response:
Um, it's definitely gotten noticeably worse recently. Like, it's been going on at this really disruptive level for about two years and two months now. That was when my company went through this huge readjustment phase, and they completely changed how our shoots and edit reviews run. 

They brought in this entirely new workflow system, and honestly, the software they make us use now is just... it's so clunky. The interface is this hideous neon purple color. My buddy Dave, who edits in the bay next to mine—well, he used to, before they made us switch to hot-desking, which is honestly the dumbest idea ever for video editors because we need our specific dual-monitor setups and our custom keyboard mapping. But Dave actually bought these special yellow-tinted glasses just to look at the new software. I tried them once, but they kept sliding down my nose and made me feel like I was wearing high school chemistry goggles. I hated chemistry, my teacher always smelled like mothballs and he would never let us actually mix the fun chemicals... 

Wait, sorry. The timeline, right. Yeah, so maybe I've always been a little bit scattered, but it only became this massive, job-threatening problem about two years and two months ago when they changed up the whole review process on me.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient confirms the doctor's premise about having trouble with focus and attention to details, noting they have always been 'scattered' but it recently became a 'massive, job-threatening problem'.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality, as their speech wanders from the timeline to software interfaces, a coworker, hot-desking, and a high school chemistry teacher before catching themselves.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in school as a kid, did teachers or your parents ever mention that you had trouble paying attention, or that you were restless or fidgety, or did you struggle with organizing your work back then?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, definitely. Even way back in elementary school, my teachers were constantly moving my desk around. I was just always out of my seat, or I'd blurt out answers, or I'd be bothering my classmates before I even realized I was doing it. 

I think it was third grade? Mrs. Gable's class. She ended up putting my desk right next to hers at the very front of the room. She had this massive obsession with owls, by the way. Like, her whole desk was covered in these little ceramic owl figurines, and she had this giant poster of a barn owl that said "Whooo's Ready to Learn?" It was honestly so creepy. Barn owls have those flat faces, you know? Like little satellite dishes. My sister and I went to a bird sanctuary a few years ago and they had one, and it just stared right through my soul. We actually went there because my sister is super into bird watching, she bought these crazy expensive binoculars that cost more than some of my actual camera lenses. Which is wild to me, because she only uses them on the weekends, whereas I need my gear to pay my rent... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, so I was always getting moved away from the other kids because I couldn't stay in my seat or keep quiet.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about owls and binoculars before losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they were 'always out of my seat' and 'couldn't stay in my seat' during class.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient notes that as a child they would 'blurt out answers' in class.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions 'bothering my classmates before I even realized I was doing it,' indicating intrusive behavior.
